title: CORF-GS: Real-Time Wireless Radiance Field Reconstruction via Coupled Optical-RF Gaussian Splatting

images.desc:
III Preliminaries



Figure 1: The workflow of CORF-GS. CORF-GS constructs a coupled Gaussian representation for optical and RF with shared geometry and modality-specific appearance.
When a new keyframe arrives, CORF-GS first employs optical-guided Gaussian expansion in under-represented regions. Since relying solely on optical guidance may neglect RF-informative areas, CORF-GS then performs coupled optical-RF optimization to jointly refine the shared Gaussians.



III-A Wireless Channel Modeling



In wireless communications, RF signals propagate from a TX to an RX through interacting with the surrounding environment. Formally, the wireless channel is characterized as a superposition of multi-path components:




𝐇​(τ)=∑l=1Lβl​𝐚r​(Ωlr)​𝐚tH​(Ωlt)​δ​(τ−τl),\mathbf{H}(\tau)=\sum_{l=1}^{L}\beta_{l}\mathbf{a}_{\mathrm{r}}(\Omega^{\mathrm{r}}_{l})\mathbf{a}_{\mathrm{t}}^{H}(\Omega^{\mathrm{t}}_{l})\delta(\tau-\tau_{l}),

(1)


where LL is the number of propagation paths; βl∈ℂ\beta_{l}\in\mathbb{C} and τl\tau_{l} denote the path gain and delay of the ll-th path, respectively. The vectors 𝐚r​(Ωlr)\mathbf{a}_{\mathrm{r}}(\Omega^{\mathrm{r}}_{l}) and 𝐚t​(Ωlt)\mathbf{a}_{\mathrm{t}}(\Omega^{\mathrm{t}}_{l}) represent the RX and TX antenna array responses, parameterized by the angle-of-arrival (AoA) Ωlr\Omega^{\mathrm{r}}_{l} and angle-of-departure (AoD) Ωlt\Omega^{\mathrm{t}}_{l}.


Conventional channel modeling relies on exhaustive grid-based measurements across the 3D space. In contrast, the efficient WRF ℱrf\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{rf}} represents propagation contributors and models power distribution with RF-specific Gaussians.
When querying ℱrf\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{rf}} at a given RX pose 𝐏r\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{r}}, a spatial spectrum 𝐒^\hat{\mathbf{S}} is rendered by ℛrf\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{rf}} to characterize the angular power distribution of the received signals:




𝐒^​(𝐏r)=ℛrf​(ℱrf;𝐏r).\hat{\mathbf{S}}(\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{r}})=\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{rf}}(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{rf}};\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{r}}).

(2)


Here, ℛrf\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{rf}} follows the same differentiable splatting process as optical 3DGS. Each RF spectrum can be preprocessed into a perspective RF image compatible with the 3DGS camera model [31].




III-B 3D Gaussian Splatting



3DGS reconstructs a scene using a set of optimizable, anisotropic 3D Gaussian primitives, enabling efficient and high-fidelity novel view synthesis. The ORF is reconstructed with NN Gaussians, and each primitive 𝒢i\mathcal{G}_{i} is parameterized by its spatial center 𝝁i∈ℝ3\boldsymbol{\mu}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, covariance matrix 𝚺i∈ℝ3×3\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}, opacity oio_{i}, and view-dependent color cic_{i}:




𝒢i={𝝁i,𝚺i,oi,ci},ℱopt≜{𝒢i}i=1N.\mathcal{G}_{i}=\{\boldsymbol{\mu}_{i},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{i},o_{i},c_{i}\},\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{opt}}\triangleq\{\mathcal{G}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}.

(3)


The spatial distribution of the ii-th Gaussian at a 3D position 𝐱∈ℝ3\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} is defined as:




Gi​(𝐱)=exp⁡(−12​(𝐱−𝝁i)⊤​𝚺i−1​(𝐱−𝝁i)).G_{i}(\mathbf{x})=\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{i})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{i}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{i})\right).

(4)




For rendering, these 3D Gaussians are projected onto the 2D image plane given a specific camera pose 𝐏c\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{c}}, and the rendering operator ℛopt​(⋅)\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{opt}}(\cdot) synthesizes the image 𝐈^\hat{\mathbf{I}}:




𝐈^​(𝐏c)=ℛopt​(ℱopt;𝐏c),\hat{\mathbf{I}}(\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{c}})=\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{opt}}(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{opt}};\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{c}}),

(5)


where the color of a target pixel 𝐮∈𝐈^\mathbf{u}\in\hat{\mathbf{I}} is accumulated via α\alpha-blending:




C​(𝐮)=∑i=1Nαi​(𝐮)​ci​∏j=1i−1(1−αj​(𝐮)).C(\mathbf{u})=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\alpha_{i}(\mathbf{u})c_{i}\prod_{j=1}^{i-1}\left(1-\alpha_{j}(\mathbf{u})\right).

(6)


Here, αi​(𝐮)=oi​gi​(𝐮)\alpha_{i}(\mathbf{u})=o_{i}g_{i}(\mathbf{u}), and gi​(𝐮)g_{i}(\mathbf{u}) denotes the projected 2D Gaussian weight evaluated at pixel 𝐮\mathbf{u}. The Gaussians are optimized by minimizing the reconstruction error between the rendered views and ground-truth images.

IV-E2 Coupled Optical-RF Optimization


CORF-GS jointly optimizes the shared geometry {𝝁,𝚺}\{\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\} and the modality-specific appearance attributes {oopt,copt}\{o^{\mathrm{opt}},c^{\mathrm{opt}}\} and {orf,crf}\{o^{\mathrm{rf}},c^{\mathrm{rf}}\} in the same optimization step. Let λrf\lambda_{\mathrm{rf}} denote the weighting factor that balances the ORF and WRF reconstruction objectives. Consequently, the overall training objective is:




ℒ=ℒopt+λrf​ℒrf,\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{opt}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{rf}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rf}},

(20)




Figure 2: Optical-RF LoG response comparison. Optical LoG responses highlight fine-grained visual structures, whereas RF LoG responses reveal RF-informative regions that are not always aligned with optical edges, motivating coupled optical-RF optimization.


This coupled optimization is crucial since the incrementally spawned Gaussians are initially guided by optical observations. Although images provide rich structural cues, the optically initialized Gaussian geometry may overlook RF-informative regions due to wavelength-dependent propagation discrepancies, as shown in Fig. 2. Compared to two-stage optimization pipelines [31, 24], CORF-GS allows RF spectra to adjust the shared geometry by coupling optical and RF supervision, preventing the WRF from passively adapting to a frozen optical geometry.

V-A1 Dataset


We evaluate CORF-GS on an open-source optical-RF dataset [31]. This dataset is built upon a digital replica of a 14×1514\times 15 m2 lobby at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The optical images are rendered using Blender, while the RF spectra are simulated via Sionna RT [4]. The carrier frequency is set to 60 GHz. The TX is equipped with a single antenna, while the RX utilizes an 8×88\times 8 planar antenna array. To construct spatial spectra, multi-path components are first mapped to angular domain and subsequently reorganized using a Jet color map and aligned with a pinhole camera projection.


To support the evaluation of real-time WRF reconstruction, we structure the data acquisition into a sequential format. During dataset collection, the TX remains stationary while the camera-RX platform moves continuously along a predefined trajectory that loops around the lobby. This process yields a sequence of 147 keyframes in total. We reserve one keyframe every eight frames for evaluation, resulting in 19 test keyframes, and use the remaining 128 keyframes for training. For more details, please refer to Appendix A2.

V-B1 Comparison with Baselines


As shown in Fig. 3, CORF-GS produces RF spectra that are more consistent with the ground truth. In contrast, NeRF2 struggles to recover the overall power distribution. Quantitatively, Table I shows that CORF-GS achieves the best performance, with PSNRrf of 18.52 dB, SSIMrf of 0.852, and LPIPSrf of 0.239. CORF-GS requires only about 2 minutes for WRF reconstruction, considerably faster than the baselines. These results show that CORF-GS improves spectrum synthesis quality while significantly reducing the reconstruction time.




V-B2 Performance with Various Training Costs


Table II and Fig. 4 analyze the trade-off between training cost and performance. CORF-GS achieves competitive spectrum synthesis performance with only a few iterations.
However, even with 30×10330\times 10^{3} iterations, WRF-GS+ only reaches PSNRrf of 18.09 dB and costs more than two hours for WRF reconstruction.
For RF-3DGS, more RF-stage iterations improve spectrum synthesis, but the performance remains below CORF-GS under all tested configurations.
Moreover, comparing (15,10)×103(15,10)_{\times 10^{3}} with (30,10)×103(30,10)_{\times 10^{3}} shows that more optical-stage iterations do not necessarily improve WRF reconstruction, suggesting that optically optimized geometry may be suboptimal for RF modeling.




V-B3 Performance with Extra Fine-tuning


Table III reports the performance of CORF-GS under different numbers of fine-tuning iterations. As the number of fine-tuning iterations increases, the quality of both optical image and RF spectrum synthesis improves, while the RF performance consistently remains better than that of RF-3DGS. With only 75 additional fine-tuning iterations, CORF-GS achieves comparable optical reconstruction quality to RF-3DGS, while requiring only about 33% of its reconstruction time. These results indicate that fine-tuning provides an optional accuracy-efficiency trade-off. It can be applied when higher ORF fidelity is required, while the real-time stage already achieves superior WRF performance with low reconstruction time.
